text: How many players do you think have a legit GOAT argument? I'll give you mine. The NBA GOAT debate is the age-old question but it's just beating a dead horse at this point. So, I'm saying who do you think has a legit argument to be the GOAT? Here are mine: Jordan- 6/6 Finals, highest PPG ever, 2x more FMVP'S than anybody else, best perimeter defender ever, majority considered the GOAT. Kareem- Most points ever, 6 rings, 6 MVPs, was all-NBA caliber for almost 20 years. LeBron- widely regarded as the best passing non-PG ever, 8 straight Finals appearances, 3 rings in 9 appearances, longevity is nearly getting to Kareem's level. Russell- 11 rings, in my opinion the best defender ever, best winner in sports history. Those are my 4 no-brainers. The weird thing about this argument is that it's not in order of best players, at least for me. For instance, I think Magic is the 4th best player ever, but he's not on this list. Here we'll get into my next tier that I'm on the fence about maybe having a legit GOAT argument: Wilt: best statistical peak ever, averaged 50 points and 26 rebounds in a season, however, historically slowed down in the postseason and only won 2 rings. Shaq: he or wilt are considered as the most dominant player ever, in my opinion best finals series ever in 2000 (38 and 17, FMVP, win in 6), 4 rings (3-peat from 2000-02), led the league in FG% 10 times. You guys probably have beef with me for not including Kobe, Magic, Duncan, and Bird in this list. But honestly, I don't think they have a legit GOAT argument. Comment if you disagree!
label: analysis

text: I use a very arbitrary judgement. After a decade, longevity doesn't mean anything to me. I of course would never value a 3 year career as a GOAT candidate, but when guys are 10, 12, 13, 15, seasons in, hitting 20 doesn't factor in at all. Ditto for Kareem. Jason Kidd is also never viewed as a better shooter than Peja Stojakovic even with more total made 3s. I value it, but after the more than a decade mark, I toss it out. Others may weight it more heavily. Peak factors in greatly, but it can't be too short. Perfect case is MJ vs Shaq. Both have to me, the 2 highest peaks in the modern era ever. Shaq's was much shorter than MJ though so while I love using peak, length of it usually comes into play, but I still value the intensity of it more than a total length being the defining factor. I factor in skills, winning, domination over your peers, being the 1st option/second option, did you make your teammates better and help them grow vs blockbuster trades/Free agency?, Peak, per game rates, efficiency, volume, two way player? I factor in a lot. Some times things can weigh more in one case but not another. Greatness is very subjective.

text: I'd say there are only two serious candidates and we all know which two I'm talking about. It can't possibly be anyone before Jordan because the concept of "GOAT" was invented to elevate Jordan above those who came before him. There were rivalries between Bird and Magic, Russell and Chamberlain, and obviously debates between them, but nobody talked about "greatest of all time" before Jordan. Starting in the late 90 and into the 00's there's a consensus on Jordan, which very strongly implies that he surpassed the players before him while no one came close to surpassing him for quite some time. In fact the narrative during that period wasn't whether anyone would ever surpass Jordan but rather whether there would be "the next Jordan". Kobe Bryant was probably the best direct replica but in his prime, nobody seriously thought he was better than the original. Some of this also spilled over into the early perceptions of LeBron James. LeBron has meanwhile cemented himself firmly in the status of "greatest since Jordan" at the bare minimum. He was good enough that we all shut up about "the next Jordan" because we were satisfied with the first LeBron. And watching LeBron throughout his career does make it hard to imagine anyone being an even greater player. Now that LeBron has managed to open the debate, there are a ton of people wading in with respect for the pre-Jordan era as well. And I think that era deserves some respect, though of everyone from that era the only one I think might approach MJ's greatness was Bill Russell. But ultimately, there was no question about it being anyone other than Jordan until LeBron came around, which is what makes LeBron the only true contender.

text: Well first and foremost because those are the primary statistics by which defenders are to be judged in the NBA. You are more than welcome to come up with a better stat for ranking defenses, but until then we have to rely on blocks, steals, rebounds as measurements of defensive prowess. You are welcome to throw in charges drawn, tips, jump balls forced and any other easily counted in game statistic you want if you can find the data. Further, to the fact that Duncan made 15 defensive appearances is a bit like Lebron making 10 straight Finals. It's impressive on its surface, but also betrays a lack of competition. The reason Hakeem or Dikembe Mutumbo or David Robinson did not make 15 all defensive first team selections is because they were all competing with one another. Duncan and Pop cheated the system by insisting Duncan was a Forward, which has two slots on the all nba defensive first team team instead of just the one for center, so instead of Duncan and KG splitting selections the way Hakeem/Mutumbo/Robinson had to they could both be selected, leading to more total selections. Kobe, MJ, Gary Payton, and KG had more FIRST team (9) selections than Duncan (8) which is a better route given both guards and forwards each had the same number of slots to compete for but with centers it's not really a fair comparison given Duncan had four opportunities to make the 1st or 2nd team while a guy like Dwight Howard or Alonzo Mourning only had 2 chances to make it.

text: The problem with those is they end up hurting your argument. If we're going with Defensive Win Shares, clearly Bill Russell is the greatest defender of all time. If we're going with Defensive Rating, David Robinson is 4th all time and was Duncan's front court teammate, which hurts his case. (And I sincerely doubt anyone is going to make the case that Dave Cowens or Gar Heard are the greatest defensive players in NBA history). If you want to go Defensive Plus/Minus, it's David Robinson again which continues to hurt Duncan's case. Duncan is 12th behind Kawhi Leonard at #11 which also hurts. The overall point here is that the advanced stats are all frought with their own problems so trying to use one of them as the end all be all argument will never work and they are too different from each other for a clear consensus to be drawn from them as a whole (other than the Admiral being severely underrated) so it's best to start with the traditional stats of points, assists, rebounds, blocks, steals as those were the traditional measures of a players' worth and if two players are too close in those areas to make a clear judgement, advanced stats can be called in to try to set one ahead of the other but going backwards and starting with advanced stats is only going to yield you arguing for Gar Heard as the best defender in NBA history.
